finding.ct_logs.internal_names: {count} internal or pre-production name(s) appear in the public certificate logs: {examples}.
finding.ct_logs.many_issuers: {count} different certificate authorities issued certificates for this domain over the last 12 months: check that this issuance is intended.
module.ct_logs.checks: Lists the public certificates issued for the domain and its subdomains from the Certificate Transparency logs (crt.sh, Cert Spotter fallback): issuing authorities, issuance rate, exposed names, and internal or pre-production names visible to everyone.
module.ct_logs.fix:
For each exposed internal or pre-production name: check whether it is reachable from the Internet and, if so, remove it from public access (delete the public DNS record, close the port, or allow access only through a VPN or authentication). An entry in the public logs can never be erased: only the host's exposure can be reduced.
Stop requesting public certificates for internal names: use an internal certificate authority, or a wildcard certificate (`*.example.com`) which does not publish every hostname. Then protect its private key with care, since it serves all the subdomains.
Review the listed certificates and authorities: for each unexpected certificate or authority, ask the team, the contractor, the host or the CDN whether they requested it. If nobody recognises it, ask the authority to revoke it, then look for the cause: a compromised ACME account or DNS access, a forgotten subdomain pointing to a third-party service.
Restrict which authorities may issue with a DNS CAA record (see the snippet, replace `letsencrypt.org` with your authority's identifier) and set a reporting address (`iodef`) where authorities may report refused requests.
If five or more authorities issued in 12 months: keep only one or two, remove the tools and accounts that use others (old ACME scripts, third-party services no longer needed) and record who requests certificates.
Monitor continuously: subscribe to an alert on new certificates for the domain (free Certificate Transparency monitors, or a service from the host or CDN) or query `crt.sh` regularly with the curl command in the snippet.
module.ct_logs.fix_snippet:
# DNS
example.com.  3600  IN  CAA  0 issue "letsencrypt.org"
example.com.  3600  IN  CAA  0 iodef "mailto:security@example.com"

# curl
curl -s "https://crt.sh/?q=%25.example.com&output=json"
module.ct_logs.title: Certificate history (Certificate Transparency)
module.ct_logs.why: Every public certificate is published: an attacker finds forgotten or internal subdomains there, and the organisation can spot unexpected issuance (an unplanned authority, a certificate nobody requested).
